## Question

Proton exchange membrane electrolyzers need an anode catalyst for the [oxygen evolution reaction](/papers/topics/oxygen-evolution-reaction/) (OER) that survives strongly acidic conditions, and today that means scarce and costly IrO2. RuO2 is more active and Ru is more abundant and cheaper, but Ru over-oxidizes to soluble species during OER and the catalyst dissolves. Earlier doping and strain strategies improved activity but stability stayed at a few hours above 10 mA cm<sup>-2</sup>. The paper asks whether a machine learning screen of mixed rutile oxides for acid stability can point to RuO2-based compositions that dissolve more slowly while staying active ([Abed et al. 2024](/papers/abed2024/)).

## Approach

A crystal graph convolutional neural network with hyperparameter tuning and dropout-based uncertainty (CGCNN-HD) was trained on 36,465 metal oxide bulk structures from the Materials Project to predict formation energy per atom, which the authors use as a proxy for Pourbaix decomposition energy (ΔG<sub>pbx</sub>). All structures were pre-scaled with a bond-statistics lattice scaling method instead of DFT relaxation, so the model works from unrelaxed hypothetical structures. To limit errors from non-ideal structures, predictions were shifted within a 95% confidence interval (μ - 2s) rather than using the dropout mean, accepting a few extra false positives for throughput. Substituting 46 elements into the rutile (space group 136) lattice gave 2070 hypothetical oxides; 195 survived an energy above hull cutoff of 0.5 eV. For Ru-containing candidates, metal-oxygen covalency from crystal orbital Hamilton population analysis served as a second stability descriptor.

Ru-Cr-Ti oxides were then made by sol-gel synthesis and characterized by XRD, HRTEM, EDS, XANES/EXAFS (including in situ XAS), STXM spectroptychography, ICP-AES dissolution measurements and 18O-labeled differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS). Surface Pourbaix diagrams and OER intermediates on rutile (110) and (101) slabs were computed with the automated WhereWulff workflow.

## Key findings

The surrogate predicted ΔG<sub>pbx</sub> with a mean absolute error of 77 meV per atom from unrelaxed structures, checked against DFT on a subset of 676 oxides covering 26 elements (34% of the data set). Ti doping lowered ΔG<sub>pbx</sub> relative to RuO2 and gave the largest covalency gain (+10.7%), ahead of Sn (+9.05%) and Ge (~~8.6%); Cr also improved Pourbaix stability. Experimentally, 25 at.% Cr cut the overpotential at 10 mA cm<sup>-2</sup> by about 70 mV relative to RuO<sub>x</sub>, while higher Cr contents formed less active Cr2O3. At most 20 at.% Ti could be incorporated, giving Ru0.6Cr0.2Ti0.2O<sub>x</sub>, which kept the rutile structure with all cations near 4~~.

Adding Ti raised the overpotential by only about 12 mV, Tafel slopes were similar (58, 56 and 54 mV dec<sup>-1</sup> for the Ti-doped, Cr-doped and RuO<sub>x</sub> samples), and Ru mass activities at 1.48 V vs RHE were 475, 433 and 79 A g<sub>Ru</sub><sup>-1</sup>, so Cr drove the activity gain (partly via about a 7-fold larger surface area). In a PEM electrolyzer at 100 mA cm<sup>-2</sup>, RuO<sub>x</sub> and Ru0.75Cr0.25O<sub>x</sub> failed within roughly 40 h, whereas the Ti-containing catalyst ran 200 h with about a 5 mV rise in cell voltage; the abstract reports 267 mV overpotential and a degradation rate of 25 μV h<sup>-1</sup>. A three-electrode test ran 1100 h at 10 mA cm<sup>-2</sup> with a 36 mV rise in the first 100 h and about 8 μV h<sup>-1</sup> thereafter. Ru dissolved about 20 times more slowly than from RuO<sub>x</sub>, staying below 1 wt% loss. Post-reaction imaging showed a hydrous Cr-O overlayer, judged not to aid stability, while in situ XAS and STXM indicated a strong Ti-O network and higher metal-oxygen covalency (computed 93.62% versus 85.20% for RuO2). DEMS showed Ti suppressed lattice oxygen participation by about 66% relative to the Cr-only catalyst. In DFT, the (110) theoretical overpotentials were 0.52, 0.66, 0.58 and 0.39 V for RuO2, RuTiO4, RuCrO4 and RuCrTiO<sub>x</sub>, and the (101) RuCrO4 value was 0.24 V, attributed to a Ru-O-Cr dimer that weakens an intra OH\*…O\* hydrogen bond and destabilizes OH\*.

The figure captions name a Ru0.6Cr0.4O<sub>x</sub> sample where the text discusses Ru0.75Cr0.25O<sub>x</sub>; this summary follows the text.

## Significance

The work shows a full loop from a graph network stability screen through synthesis to long-duration electrolyzer testing, and it separates roles: Ti supplies stability through covalency and a rigid oxide framework that slows Ru dissolution and lattice oxygen evolution, while Cr supplies activity. It supports metal-oxygen covalency as a practical descriptor for acid-stable oxide design.
